# Overview

This workflow illustrates how the **RDynLib infrastructure supports metabolite structural annotation**, from spectral data exploration and comparison to the recording of compound annotations and their provenance in DynLib databases.

A flax seed DynLib database, generated from a new LC-MS experiment containing compounds to be structurally annotated, serves as the **query database** throughout the workflow.
It is compared with a maize DynLib database containing previously characterized metabolites and their associated spectra, which serves as the **reference database**.

The workflow progresses from general **spectral similarity searching** against a reference DynLib database (the maize database in this example) and the **export of spectral data for further analysis with external databases and tools**, to detailed comparison and **visualization of individual spectra**, including **matching across different MSⁿ levels**.
A key functionality of RDynLib is the **joint exploitation of complementary fragmentation information acquired on different mass spectrometry platforms**, such as ion trap and QTOF instruments, to support structural characterization.
Biochemical and spectral relationships are explored through the construction and visualization of **CSPP and GNPS-like molecular networks**.

Finally, the resulting **compound annotation is written to the flaxseed DynLib database**.
Along with the structural annotation itself, the evidence and reasoning underlying the characterization are recorded as an **annotation event**, preserving the provenance of the annotation and documenting the justification for the **assigned confidence level**.

# Workflow setup

## Loading required packages

```{r}
#| message: false
#| results: "hide"
#| warning: false
#| 
library(devtools)
library(DBI)
library(RSQLite)
library(Spectra)
library(here)
library(CompoundDb)
library(MsBackendMgf)
library(scales)
library(readr)
# TODO: Replace with library(RDynLib) once the package is finalized.
load_all()
```

## Retrieving DynLib datasets from Zenodo

The DynLib SQLite databases used in this workflow are available on Zenodo. Before running the chunk below, download the databases using the code in `00_Download_Dynlib_databases.qmd`.
Each database contains the features detected in one or more LC-MS experiments together with their associated mass spectral data and experimental metadata and compound annotations.
Separate databases are used for each mass spectrometry platform and ionization mode:

-   **FTneg / FTpos**: LTQ-Orbitrap FT-MS data acquired in negative / positive ionization mode, including MSⁿ spectra
-   **QTOFneg / QTOFpos**: QTOF-MS data acquired in negative / positive ionization mode, including MS/MS spectra

```{r}
#| message: false
#| results: "hide"
#| warning: false

data_dir <- here::here("data")
zenodo_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "zenodo")

ftneg_path   <- file.path(data_dir, "DYL_FLAX_herba_FTMSneg.sqlite")
ftpos_path   <- file.path(data_dir, "DyLib_FTMS_pos.sqlite")
qtofneg_path <- file.path(data_dir, "DYL_FLAX_QTOFneg.sqlite")
qtofpos_path <- file.path(data_dir, "DyLib_QTOF_pos.sqlite")

maize_ftneg   <- file.path(zenodo_dir, "maize_ftneg.sqlite")
maize_ftpos   <- file.path(zenodo_dir, "maize_ftpos.sqlite")
maize_qtofneg <- file.path(zenodo_dir, "maize_qtofneg.sqlite")
flax_ftneg    <- file.path(zenodo_dir, "flax_ftneg.sqlite")
flax_qtofneg  <- file.path(zenodo_dir, "flax_qtofneg.sqlite")
hdg_ftneg     <- file.path(zenodo_dir, "hdg_ftneg.sqlite")

inputs <- c(
    ftneg_path, ftpos_path, qtofneg_path,
    maize_ftneg, maize_ftpos, maize_qtofneg,
    flax_ftneg, flax_qtofneg, hdg_ftneg
)
missing_inputs <- inputs[!file.exists(inputs)]

if (length(missing_inputs) > 0L) {
    stop("Missing databases: ", paste(missing_inputs, collapse = ", "))
}

connect_dynlib <- function(path) {
    DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), path)
}

con_ftneg   <- connect_dynlib(ftneg_path)
con_ftpos   <- connect_dynlib(ftpos_path)
con_qtofneg <- connect_dynlib(qtofneg_path)
con_mftneg  <- connect_dynlib(maize_ftneg)
con_mftpos  <- connect_dynlib(maize_ftpos)
con_mqtneg  <- connect_dynlib(maize_qtofneg)
con_fft     <- connect_dynlib(flax_ftneg)
con_fqt     <- connect_dynlib(flax_qtofneg)
con_hdgft   <- connect_dynlib(hdg_ftneg)
```

## Prepare the FTneg reference

Merge the maize and HDG databases. Both store retention times in minutes.

```{r}
target_DL_FTneg <- file.path(output_dir, "FTneg_maize_hdg.sqlite")
merge_databases(
    main_db = maize_ftneg, add_db = hdg_ftneg,
    output_db = target_DL_FTneg, convert_add_rt = FALSE
)
sp_maize_hdg <- sql_to_spectra(target_DL_FTneg)
sp_ftflax <- sql_to_spectra(flax_ftneg)
sp_qtmaize <- sql_to_spectra(maize_qtofneg)
sp_qtflax <- sql_to_spectra(flax_qtofneg)
```

# Batch spectral similarity against DynLib

Each search selects its query and reference MS levels and spectrum types independently. For the combined DynLib summary, retain hits with a similarity score of at least 0.70 and at least four matched peaks. Count hit rows, distinct query spectra, and distinct flaxseed compounds separately.

## Flaxseed FTneg vs. maize and HDG FTneg

### Inspect the spectra

Use `spectraData()` to count query spectra and inspect the available MS levels and spectrum types. For the reference MS² count, keep individual spectra with assigned compound names.

```{r}
ft_metadata <- spectraData(sp_ftflax, columns = c("spectrum_type", "msLevel"))
table(ft_metadata$spectrum_type, ft_metadata$msLevel)

ft_reference <- as.data.frame(spectraData(
    sp_maize_hdg, columns = c("msLevel", "spectrum_type", "name")
))
ft_reference$name <- trimws(ft_reference$name)
nrow(subset(
    ft_reference,
    msLevel == 2L & spectrum_type == "individual" &
        !is.na(name) & name != "" & toupper(name) != "NULL" &
        !startsWith(name, "!")
))
```

### MS2 vs. MS2

In the FT-MSⁿ data of the present target and the query libraries, MS2 precursor masses are measured at high resolution, whereas the fragment ions in both the query and target spectra were acquired at unit resolution in the ion trap of the hybrid FT mass spectrometer.
We set `requirePrecursor = TRUE` with `ppm = 5` and `tolerance = 0`, and set `fragments_resolution = "unit.resolution"`.
The `ppm` and `tolerance` parameters are then only applied to the precursor matching.

```{r}
ftms_matches2_T <- similarity_RDynLib_match(
  sp_ftflax,
  sp_maize_hdg,
  polarity_query = 0,
  polarity_target = 0,
  msLevel_query = 2,
  msLevel_target = 2,
  spectrum_type_query = "individual",
  spectrum_type_target = "individual",
  requirePrecursor = TRUE,
  tolerance = 0,
  ppm = 5,
  threshold = 0.7,
  fragments_resolution = "unit.resolution"
 )

#Order the MS2-MS2 matches and  them according to decreasing similarity score and number of matched peaks.
names(ftms_matches2_T)
nrow(ftms_matches2_T)
o <- order(ftms_matches2_T$matched_peaks_count, decreasing =T)
print(ftms_matches2_T[o,c("query_compound_id", "query_spectrum_id", "msLevel","precursorMz","target_name","target_msLevel","target_precursorMz","target_compound_id","score", "matched_peaks_count")])
```

We can save the spectral matching results as .csv file for later consultation.
To do so, we select the relevant columns from the similarity search output and optionally add metadata, such as the query date, the databases used, and the matching parameters.
Recording this information allows us to subsequently combine results from different similarity searches, potentially involving different databases, spectrum types, MS levels, or matching parameters.
This facilitates the comparison, interpretation, and integration of results across multiple searches.

```{r}
# Select the variable of interest to save
(matches_table <- (ftms_matches2_T[o,c("query_compound_id", "query_compound_accession","query_spectrum_id", "msLevel","precursorMz","target_name","target_msLevel","target_precursorMz","target_compound_id","target_compound_accession","target_spectrum_id","score", "matched_peaks_count")]))

# Extend the table with metadata about the Query (date of query, query database, target databases)

# Retrieve the experiment accession
experiment_accession <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con_fft, "SELECT experiment_accession FROM experiment")

# Assemble the table
matches_table_assembled <- data.frame(experiment = experiment_accession, queryDate = "2009/09/30", queryDB = "flax_FTneg2023", targetDB ="maize_hdg_FTneg", matches_table)

# Export to a .csv file
write.csv(matches_table_assembled, here("data","matches_ftms_flaxseed_MS2_individual_vs_maizehdg_MS2_individual.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

```

Number of hits with a score higher or equal to 0.7 and a minimun matched_peaks_count of 4
```{r}
strong_matches <- subset(
    ftms_matches2_T,
    score >= 0.7 & matched_peaks_count >= 4
)

nrow(strong_matches)                             
length(unique(strong_matches$query_spectrum_id))
```

Six query spectra yielded a perfect similarity score of 1, with more than five matched spectral peaks (matching m/z of fragments or neutral losses).
We store the `compound_id`s of compounds for which a strong match was found, for later use.

```{r}
flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS2MS2 <- ftms_matches2_T$query_compound_id[o][1:6]
flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS2MS2
```

The `add_spectral_matches()` function allows to **store spectral matches**, or a selected subset, in dedicated columns of the `msms_spectrum` table of the DynLib SQL database.

However, storing new matching results will overwrite any previously stored results for the corresponding query spectra.
We are curious to know whether matching results already exist for the six spectra identified above.

Using their `query_spectrum_id` values, and a simple R code through the existing spectra object `sp_ftflax`, created from the flax_ftneg DynLib database. We display only the spectrum identifier (spectrum_id) and the available spectral matching fields.

In thin chunk we store those best six matches in the flax ftneg SQL database (and overwrite existing matches if present):

```{r}
query_ids <- head(ftms_matches2_T$query_spectrum_id[o], 6L)

# Make a selection of the spectral similarity output table
ftms_matches_sel <- ftms_matches2_T[o,][1:6,]

# Add the selection of matches to the msms_spectrum table of the sql database
add_spectral_matches(con_fft, ftms_matches_sel)

# Reload the Spectra object to inspect the updated metadata.
sp_ftflax <- sql_to_spectra(flax_ftneg)
query_ids <- unique(ftms_matches_sel$query_spectrum_id)

columns <- c("spectrum_id","match_name","match_compound_id","match_precursor_mz","match_score","match_common","match_mslevel","match_spectrum_type")

spectrum_metadata <- as.data.frame(spectraData(
    sp_ftflax, columns = intersect(columns, spectraVariables(sp_ftflax))
))

rows <- match(query_ids, spectrum_metadata$spectrum_id)
spectrum_metadata[rows[!is.na(rows)], , drop = FALSE]
```


### MS3(query) vs. MS2(target)

In the FT-MSⁿ data, first order fragmentation may correspond to the dissociation of an adduct, so that only the second order fragmentation becomes structurally informative.
Alternatively, higher order fragmentation spectra may correspond to the fragmentation of a substructure that can exist independently in a reference database.
Therefore it can be highly of interest to match also higher order fragmentation spectra against a reference database.
As an example of a comparison involving higher order MS levels, we search the MS3 flaxseed spectra against the MS2 spectra of the reference DynLib.
Because `fragments_resolution = "unit.resolution"`, the `ppm` and `tolerance` parameters apply only to the precursor matching, and because the precursor m/z values associated with the MS3 spectra are recorded at unit resolution, we use a larger absolute precursor mass tolerance.

```{r}
ftms_matches32_T <- similarity_RDynLib_match(
  sp_ftflax,
  sp_maize_hdg,
  polarity_query = 0,
  polarity_target = 0,
  msLevel_query = 3,
  msLevel_target = 2,
  spectrum_type_query = "individual",
  spectrum_type_target = "individual",
  requirePrecursor = TRUE,
  tolerance = 0.5,
  ppm = 5,
  threshold = 0.7,
  fragments_resolution = "unit.resolution"
)

#Order the MS3-MS2 matches and  them according to decreasing similarity score and number of matched peaks.
nrow(ftms_matches32_T)
o <- order(ftms_matches32_T$matched_peaks_count, decreasing =T)
strong_matches <- subset(
    ftms_matches32_T,
    score >= 0.7 & matched_peaks_count >= 4
)
nrow(strong_matches)                             
length(unique(strong_matches$query_spectrum_id))
```

30 query MS3 spectra yielded similarity score of \>0.7, with five or more matched spectral peaks.
We store the `compound_id`s of unique compounds for which a strong match was found, for later use.

```{r}
flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS3MS2 <- unique(ftms_matches32_T$query_compound_id[o][1:30])
```


### MS3(query) vs MS3(target)
Matching MS3 spectra against MS3 reference spectra can reveal similarities between fragment ions originating from different precursor compounds. 
Here, the MS3 spectra from flaxseed FT-MSⁿ data were compared against the MS3 spectra of the reference DynLib. This comparison yielded 127 spectral matches (similarity score ≥ 0.7), involving 103 unique flaxseed compounds and 90 unique reference compounds. The matched reference compounds included flavonoid glycosides, phenolic acid derivatives, lignin-related compounds, and other specialized metabolites.
These results illustrate the potential of higher-order spectral matching to identify structural similarities between metabolites and provide complementary information for compound annotation. However, MS3 spectral similarity alone does not establish the identity of the intact compound or confirm the presence of a specific substructure.

```{r}
ftms_matches33_T <- similarity_RDynLib_match(
  sp_ftflax,
  sp_maize_hdg,
  polarity_query = 0,
  polarity_target = 0,
  msLevel_query = 3,
  msLevel_target = 3,
  spectrum_type_query = "individual",
  spectrum_type_target = "individual",
  requirePrecursor = TRUE,
  tolerance = 0.5,
  ppm = 5,
  threshold = 0.7,
  fragments_resolution = "unit.resolution"
)

#Verify how many important individual reference-library hits found
nrow(ftms_matches33_T)
o <- order(ftms_matches33_T$matched_peaks_count, decreasing =T)

strong_matches <- subset(
    ftms_matches33_T,
    score >= 0.7 & matched_peaks_count >= 4
)

nrow(strong_matches)                             
length(unique(strong_matches$query_spectrum_id))
```

26 query MS3 spectra yielded similarity score >0.9, with five or more matched spectral peaks.
We store the `compound_id`s of unique compounds for which a strong match was found, for later use.

```{r}
flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS3MS3 <- unique(ftms_matches33_T$query_compound_id[o][1:26])
```

## QTOF spectral similarity (flax vs maize_hdg)

### Preliminary operations and database exploration

We can apply the same batch similarity matching procedure to QTOFneg data of the flax experiment.
The target QTOFneg DynLib database contains an annotated maize experiment.
We first need to convert the query and target SQL databases to `Spectra` objects:

```{r}
sp_qtmaize <- sql_to_spectra(maize_qtofneg)
sp_qtflax <- sql_to_spectra(flax_qtofneg)
#Extract available spectrum type
available_spectrum_types(con_mqtneg) 
available_spectrum_types(con_fqt) 
```


In the flaxseed QTOFneg DynLib, two spectrum_types are available: `all_energies` and `same_energy`. These spectrum_types both represent composite spectra. The `same_energy` spectrum type combines replicate MS2 spectra acquired at the same collision energy. Since spectra were acquired at three collision energies, a chromatographic feature (`compound_id`) can be associated with up to three `same_energy` spectra, one per collision energy. The `all_energies` spectrum type combines MS2 spectra acquired at all different collision energies for a given `comound_id`.

Count the flax MS2 spectra by spectrum type.

```{r}
flax_ms2 <- filterMsLevel(sp_qtflax, 2L)
table(flax_ms2$spectrum_type)
```
Total MS2 spectra number in maize qtof negative data where the name is not null:

```{r}
maize_ms2 <- filterMsLevel(sp_qtmaize, 2L)

maize_metadata <- as.data.frame(spectraData(
    maize_ms2, columns = c("spectrum_type", "name")
))
maize_metadata$name <- trimws(maize_metadata$name)

nrow(subset(
    maize_metadata,
    spectrum_type == "individual" &
        !is.na(name) & name != "" & toupper(name) != "NULL" &
        !startsWith(name, "!")
))
```

### MS/MS same energy vs. MS/MS

We then use 'similarity_RDynLib_match()' to search the QTOF spectra from the flax experiment against the maize DynLib spectra.
Since both datasets contain high-resolution fragment ions, we set 'fragments_resolution = "high.resolution"'.
In this case, 'ppm' and 'tolerance' define the m/z tolerance used for fragment peak matching.
With 'requirePrecursor = TRUE', these parameters are also used to pre-filter target spectra based on precursor m/z.
Here, we use a tolerance of 20 ppm and no additional absolute tolerance (tolerance = 0).

```{r}
qtof_matches_samen_ind_T <- similarity_RDynLib_match(
  sp_qtflax,
  sp_qtmaize,
  polarity_query = 0,
  polarity_target = 0,
  msLevel_query = 2,
  msLevel_target = 2,
  spectrum_type_query = "same_energy",
  spectrum_type_target = "individual",
  requirePrecursor = TRUE,
  tolerance = 0,
  ppm = 20,
  threshold = 0.7,
  fragments_resolution = "high.resolution"
 )
```
Verify how many important individual reference-library hits found: 
```{r}
nrow(qtof_matches_samen_ind_T)
o <- order(qtof_matches_samen_ind_T$matched_peaks_count, decreasing =T)

strong_matches <- subset(
    qtof_matches_samen_ind_T,
    score >= 0.7 & matched_peaks_count >= 4
)

nrow(strong_matches)                             
length(unique(strong_matches$query_spectrum_id))
```

Six flaxseed MS/MS spectra yielded a hit with similarity score \> 0.7 and five or more matched spectral peaks. These include spectra acquired at different collision energies for the same chromatographic feature (`compound_id`) and therefore do not  represent six distinct compounds.
We store the `compound_id`s of unique compounds for which a strong match was found, for later use.

```{r}
flax_qtofneg_compounds_DLmatch_samen_ind <- unique(qtof_matches_samen_ind_T$query_compound_id[o][1:6])
```

Store the spectral matches in the `msms_spectrum` table of the query SQL database using the `add_spectral_matches()` from the RDynLib package:

```{r}
query_ids <- head(qtof_matches_samen_ind_T$query_spectrum_id[o], 6L)

# Make a selection of the spectral similarity output table
ftms_matches_sel <- qtof_matches_samen_ind_T[o,][1:6,]

# Add the selection of matches to the msms_spectrum table of the sql database
add_spectral_matches(con_fft, ftms_matches_sel)

# Reload the Spectra object to inspect the updated metadata.
sp_qtflax <- sql_to_spectra(flax_qtofneg)
query_ids <- unique(ftms_matches_sel$query_spectrum_id)

spectrum_metadata <- as.data.frame(spectraData(
    sp_qtflax, columns = intersect(columns, spectraVariables(sp_qtflax))
))

rows <- match(query_ids, spectrum_metadata$spectrum_id)
spectrum_metadata[rows[!is.na(rows)], , drop = FALSE]
```



### MS/MS all energies vs. MS/MS

```{r}
qtof_all_hits <- similarity_RDynLib_match(
  sp_qtflax,
  sp_qtmaize,
  polarity_query = 0,
  polarity_target = 0,
  msLevel_query = 2,
  msLevel_target = 2,
  spectrum_type_query = "all_energies",
  spectrum_type_target = "individual",
  requirePrecursor = TRUE,
  tolerance = 0,
  ppm = 20,
  threshold = 0.7,
  fragments_resolution = "high.resolution"
 )
```
There is only one match above the imposed threshold:

```{r}
o <- order(qtof_all_hits$matched_peaks_count, decreasing =T)
print(qtof_all_hits[o,c("query_compound_id", "query_spectrum_id", "msLevel","precursorMz","target_name","target_msLevel","target_precursorMz","target_compound_id","score", "matched_peaks_count")])


```

The query compound_id and match compound_id where already found using the `same_energy` spectra with similar socres (same number of matching peaks and score slightly higher when using `same_energy` spectrum (0.766 vs. 0.705).

## Public spectral database search

Export flaxseed DynLib spectra in MGF format for spectral library searches in GNPS2. RDynLib lets you select the experiments, spectrum types, and MS levels to export.

### Flaxseed FTneg DynLib
Identify the available experiments, then use spectraData() to inspect the spectrum types and MS levels. Specify spectrum_type and msLevel in the columns argument.
```{r}
# flax_ftneg is the path to the flaxseed ftneg sql DynLib
# Create Spectra and CompDb objects
sp_ftflax <- sql_to_spectra(flax_ftneg)
cdb_ftflax <- ExpCompDb(flax_ftneg)

# List the available experiments
names(compounds(cdb_ftflax))
table(compounds(cdb_ftflax, columns = "expid"))

# List available spectrum types and MS levels
spectraVariables(sp_ftflax)
spectrum_metadata <- spectraData(sp_ftflax,
  columns = c("compound_id", "spectrum_type", "msLevel")
)
type.level <- table(spectrum_metadata$spectrum_type, spectrum_metadata$msLevel)

type.level
```

The flaxseed FTneg DynLib contains multilevel fragmentation spectra acquired with ion trap instruments. The `pseudo_MS2` spectrum type (which has `ms_level` assigned to 2) combines fragment ions from all MSⁿ levels of a spectral tree into a single spectrum, summing the intensities of matching fragment ions. By integrating fragmentation information across MSⁿ levels, this `pseudo_MS2` representation may facilitate comparisons with reference MS/MS spectra, acquired using QTOF or other tandem mass spectrometers, and available in public spectral databases.

#### Pseudo Ms2
Here, we will export the `pseudo_MS2` spectra from the flaxseed FTneg DynLib database in MGF format for spectral similarity searching against public spectral databases:
```{r}
ft_pseudoMS2 <- here("data", "ft_pseudoMS2.mgf")

sql_to_mgf(
  sqlite_path = flax_ftneg,
  expid = 266,
  spectrum_type = "pseudo_MS2",
  ms_level = NULL,
  output_file = ft_pseudoMS2
)
```

The exported MGF files were submitted to **GNPS2** for spectral similarity searching against all available reference spectral libraries. In the GNPS2 **File Browser**, we created a folder and uploaded the MGF files. We then launched the **Library Search** workflow (*Launch Workflows → librarysearch_workflow*) to search the uploaded spectra against the reference libraries. Multiple MGF files can be launched simultaneously.

The `sql_to_mgf()` function writes a unique identifier, constructed by concatenating the compound_accession and spectrum_id separated by an underscore, to the SCANS field of the exported MGF file. Consequently, the #Scan# column in the resulting GNPS spectral matching reports contains this identifier, allowing the original `spectrum_id` and the associated `compound_accession` to be retrieved and linked back to the corresponding `compound_id` in the DynLib database.

The resulting spectral matches were downloaded as a CSV file for further analysis in R.

We extract the unique `compound_id`s associated with high-scoring spectral matches (MQScore >= 0.8 & SharedPeaks >= 4).
Filter matches and extract compound IDs
```{r}
# Import GNPS2 spectral matching results from TSV
gnps_matches <- read_tsv(
  "../data/matches_gnps_ft_pseudo.tsv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Filter GNPS matches by similarity criteria and spectrum file
gnps_matches_filtered <- subset(
  gnps_matches,
  MQScore >= 0.8 & SharedPeaks >= 4 &
    SpectrumFile == "ft_pseudo_MS2_MS2.mgf"
)

# Extract spectrum IDs from GNPS scan identifiers
gnps_matches_filtered$spectrum_id <- as.integer(
  sub(".*_", "", gnps_matches_filtered[["#Scan#"]])
)

# Retrieve spectrum-to-compound mapping from Spectra
spectrum_mapping <- spectraData(
  sp_ftflax, columns = c("spectrum_id", "compound_id")
)

# Associate GNPS matches with DynLib compounds
gnps_matches_filtered$compound_id <- spectrum_mapping$compound_id[
  match(gnps_matches_filtered$spectrum_id, spectrum_mapping$spectrum_id)
]

# Extract unique matched compound IDs
flax_ftneg_compounds_GNPSmatch_PseudoMS2 <- unique(gnps_matches_filtered$compound_id)
c(
    exported_query_spectra = sum(
        trimws(readLines(ft_pseudoMS2, warn = FALSE)) == "BEGIN IONS"
    ),
    qualifying_hits = nrow(gnps_matches)
)
```

We searched 395 flaxseed FTneg pseudo-MS² spectra against the GNPS2 spectral libraries and retained five hits with MQScore ≥ 0.80 and at least four shared peaks.

Inspect GNPS matches and structural annotations
```{r}
gnps_matches_filtered[, c(
  "#Scan#", "compound_id","spectrum_id", 
  "Compound_Name", "Smiles", "InChIKey",
  "MQScore", "SharedPeaks", "MZErrorPPM"
)]
```

In the DynLib export, each #Scan# value ends with `<compound_accession>_<spectrum_id>`. For example, in `RD-20260907-DNPZEQ-101007_202298`, the fourth hyphen-separated component contains compound accession `101007` and spectrum ID `202298`, separated by an underscore. In flax_ftneg, the original DynLib database, the compound accession was assigned using the compound’s local compound_id. The two values therefore coincide in this database. If the compound is imported into another DynLib, its local compound_id may change while its original accession is retained.

#### Individual Msn
In the code chunk below, we created a loop to export separate MGF files for each combination of spectrum type and MS level, for which spectra are available in the flaxseed FTneg DynLib database.
```{r}
# Export one MGF file per spectrum_type - msLevel combination

for (i in seq_len(nrow(type.level))) {
  for (j in seq_len(ncol(type.level))){

  # Skip combinations with no spectra
    if (type.level[i, j] == 0) next

    type <- rownames(type.level)[i]
    level <- colnames(type.level)[j]


  output <- here(
    "data",
    paste0("ft_", type, "_MS", level, ".mgf")
  )

  sql_to_mgf(
    sqlite_path = flax_ftneg,
    expid = 266,
    spectrum_type = type,
    ms_level = as.integer(level),
    output_file = output
  )
  }
}
```

The `sql_to_mgf()` function can also export multiple MS levels, spectrum types, and experiments into a single mgf file.

Assign expid NULL to return all the available expids in the database. (In this
case of the flax ftneg database, it will return only one experiment.)
```{r}
ft_multi <- here("data", "ft_multi_exp_types.mgf")

sql_to_mgf(
  sqlite_path = flax_ftneg,
  expid = NULL,
  spectrum_type = c("individual", "pseudo_MS2"),
  ms_level = c(2, 3, 4),
  output_file = ft_multi
)
```


Compare the individual MS2 spectra to public databases on GNPS. We set the similarity score threshold at minimum 4 shared peaks and a score of 0.8.

```{r}
#chose the tsv file 
path <- "../data/ftms_indivi_MS2_tsv.tsv"
# Import GNPS2 spectral matching results from TSV
gnps_matches <- read_tsv(
  path,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Inspect the available columns
names(gnps_matches)
head(gnps_matches)

c(
    exported_query_spectra = sum(
        trimws(readLines(ft_pseudoMS2, warn = FALSE)) == "BEGIN IONS"
    ),
    qualifying_hits = nrow(gnps_matches)
)

```
We searched 395 flaxseed FTneg with individual MS² spectra against the GNPS2 spectral libraries and retained one hit with MQScore ≥ 0.80 and at least four shared peaks.

Extract the corresponding compound_id and spectrum_id
```{r}
# Select GNPS matches meeting similarity criteria
gnps_matches_filtered2 <- gnps_matches |>
  filter(
    MQScore >= 0.8,
    SharedPeaks >= 4,
    SpectrumFile == "ft_individual_MS2.mgf"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    spectrum_id = as.integer(sub(".*_", "", `#Scan#`))
  )

# Retrieve spectrum-to-compound mapping from SQLite
spectrum_mapping <- dbGetQuery(
  con_ftneg,
  "SELECT spectrum_id, compound_id
   FROM msms_spectrum"
)

# Link GNPS matches to flaxseed compounds
gnps_matches_filtered2 <- gnps_matches_filtered2 |>
  left_join(spectrum_mapping, by = "spectrum_id")

# Inspect results
gnps_matches_filtered2 |>
  select(
    spectrum_id,
    compound_id,
    Compound_Name,
    MQScore,
    SharedPeaks
  )

# Number of unique matched flaxseed compounds
n_distinct(gnps_matches_filtered2$compound_id, na.rm = TRUE)

```

The results show that only one match was identified between spectra of the *individual* spectrum type and the public spectral libraries available through GNPS, with a similarity score of 0.94 and six shared peaks. In contrast, five matches were obtained when comparing *pseudo-MS2* spectra against the same libraries. These findings suggest that the *pseudo-MS2* representation is better suited for spectral similarity searches against public spectral libraries, as it yields a higher number of matches than the *individual* spectrum type.

### Flaxseed QTOFneg DynLib
For the flaxseed QTOFneg DynLib database, we will export first the `same_energy` spectra, and later the `all_energies` spectra, in MGF format for spectral similarity searching against public spectral databases. 

#### All_energies
The `all_energies` spectra combine fragmentation information acquired at different collision energies.
Inspect the existing expids in the database:
```{r}
get_expid(flax_qtofneg)
```

Create an mgf file for the experiment with expid = 52, corresponding to the flax qtof neg data, containing the spectra of spectrum type **all_energies**.
```{r}
#| message: false
#| results: "hide"
#| warning: false
qt_assembled <- here("data", "qt_assembled.mgf")
path <- flax_qtofneg
sql_to_mgf(path, expid = 52, spectrum_type = "all_energies", 
           output_file = qt_assembled) 

#Read the tsv file that contains the gnps matching results

# Import GNPS2 spectral matching results from TSV

  path,
  show_col_types = FALSE

# Inspect the available columns
names(gnps_matches)
head(gnps_matches)
dim(gnps_matches)

c(
    exported_query_spectra = sum(
        trimws(readLines(qt_assembled, warn = FALSE)) == "BEGIN IONS"
    ),

)
```
We searched 120 flaxseed Qtofneg with all_energies MS² spectra against the GNPS2 spectral libraries and retained 16 hit with MQScore ≥ 0.80 and in contrast to ftms we select at least six shared peaks because qtof represents a large number of peaks.
Extract the corresponding compound_id and spectrum_id
```{r}
gnps_matches_filtered_qt_all <- subset(
    gnps_matches,
    MQScore >= 0.8 & SharedPeaks >= 6 &
        SpectrumFile == "qt_assembled.mgf"
)

gnps_matches_filtered_qt_all$spectrum_id <- as.integer(
    sub(".*_", "", gnps_matches_filtered_qt_all$`#Scan#`)

length(flax_qtneg_compounds_gnpsmatch_all)
```

Using the QTOFneg all_energies spectra, we retained 16 GNPS matches with a similarity score (MQScore) of at least 0.80 and at least six shared fragment peaks. Each match mapped to a different flaxseed compound_id, yielding 16 distinct chromatographic features with putative annotations.

## Overview

Pseudo-MS² yielded more qualifying matches. Our observations corroborate a potential advantage of the use of pseudo-MS2 spectra, over the use of individual ion-trap generated MS2 spectra
For each flaxseed DynLib database (FTneg and QTOFneg), combine high-scoring matches to characterized reference DynLib compounds or GNPS spectra into a vector of unique compound_id values.
```{r}

## FTneg: Combine DynLib and GNPS matches

flax_ftneg_compounds_all_matches <- unique(c(
  flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS2MS2,
  flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS3MS2,
  flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS3MS3,
  flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS4MS2,
  flax_ftneg_compounds_DLmatch_MS4MS3,
  flax_ftneg_compounds_GNPSmatch_PseudoMS2,
  101005
))

# Remove missing IDs
flax_ftneg_compounds_all_matches <-
  flax_ftneg_compounds_all_matches[
    !is.na(flax_ftneg_compounds_all_matches)
  ]

# Number of unique FTneg compounds
n_ftneg <- length(flax_ftneg_compounds_all_matches)

## QTOFneg: Combine DynLib and GNPS matches

flax_qtofneg_compounds_all_matches <- unique(c(
  flax_qtofneg_compounds_DLmatch,
  flax_qtneg_compounds_gnpsmatch_all,
  flax_qtneg_compounds_gnpsmatch_same
))

# Remove missing IDs
flax_qtofneg_compounds_all_matches <-
  flax_qtofneg_compounds_all_matches[
    !is.na(flax_qtofneg_compounds_all_matches)
  ]

# Number of unique QTOFneg compounds
n_qtofneg <- length(flax_qtofneg_compounds_all_matches)

# Display results
cat("FTneg unique matched compounds:", n_ftneg, "\n")
cat("QTOFneg unique matched compounds:", n_qtofneg, "\n")

```


In total,62 and 19 distinct chromatographic features in the flaxseed FTneg and QTOFneg DynLib databases, respectively, yielded high-scoring spectral matches with characterized compounds in the reference DynLib or public spectral databases. 

These sets of matched compounds will subsequently be compared with the FTneg–QTOFneg alignment results to investigate the overlap between the two analytical platforms and assess the consistency of spectral annotations across datasets.

# Alignment FTneg - QTOFneg
The alignment between the flax ftms and qtof negative data is performed in the **RDynlib_alignment_sql_flax.qmd** workflow. The resulting aligned compounds are 
stored in the assoc.txt file:

```{r}
assoc_path <- here("data", "flax_qtn_ftn_align.txt")
alignment <- read.delim(assoc_path, colClasses = "character")
```

Here we extract the different statistics about the number of matches and aligned
compounds:
```{r}
# Keep one row per distinct FTneg–QTOFneg pair.
assoc <- unique(data.frame(
    ft_id = alignment$ref_compid,
    qt_id = alignment$target_compid
))

ft_high <- unique(as.character(flax_ftneg_compounds_all_matches))
qt_high <- unique(as.character(flax_qtofneg_compounds_all_matches))

# Unique IDs with a high-scoring match and at least one aligned partner.
ft_aligned <- intersect(ft_high, assoc$ft_id)
qt_aligned <- intersect(qt_high, assoc$qt_id)

# Aligned pairs with high-scoring spectral matches on both sides.
both <- subset(assoc, ft_id %in% ft_high & qt_id %in% qt_high)

# Unique IDs with a high-scoring match and no high-scoring aligned partner.
ft_only <- setdiff(ft_aligned, both$ft_id)
qt_only <- setdiff(qt_aligned, both$qt_id)

c(
    "Distinct aligned pairs" = nrow(assoc),
    "Aligned pairs with high-scoring matches on both sides" = nrow(both),
    "Unique FTneg IDs with high-scoring matches" = length(ft_high),
    "Unique QTOFneg IDs with high-scoring matches" = length(qt_high),
    "Unique FTneg IDs with a high-scoring match and an aligned partner" =
        length(ft_aligned),
    "Unique QTOFneg IDs with a high-scoring match and an aligned partner" =
        length(qt_aligned),
    "Unique FTneg IDs with a high-scoring match and no high-scoring partner" =
        length(ft_only),
    "Unique QTOFneg IDs with a high-scoring match and no high-scoring partner" =
        length(qt_only)
)

```
Display the compound_ids:
```{r}
ft_only
qt_only
both
subset(assoc, ft_id %in% ft_only | qt_id %in% qt_only)
```


Alignment of the FTneg and QTOFneg experiments revealed the complementarity of the two acquisition methods. Among the 30 aligned compound pairs, three QTOFneg compounds yielded high-scoring spectral matches exclusively from QTOF MS/MS spectra, whereas three FTneg compounds yielded high-scoring matches exclusively from ion-trap MS2 or MS3 spectra. Notably, no aligned compound pair exhibited high-scoring spectral matches in both datasets. These results highlight the complementary annotation capabilities of FT-MSⁿ and QTOF-MS/MS, suggesting that combining both acquisition methods can improve spectral annotation coverage.

# Single spectrum spectral similarity search against DynLib

Merge the query and reference databases for a compound-specific search. Resolve the accession in the merged database to obtain its local compound ID.
```{r}
#output
ftflax_maize_hdg_sql <- here("data", "ftflax_maize_hdg.sqlite")
#convert_add_rt is False because both databases are already in minutes so no need for conversion
merge_databases(main_db  = main_maize_hdg, add_db = flax_ftneg,
                output_db = ftflax_maize_hdg_sql, convert_add_rt = FALSE)

con_all <- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ftflax_maize_hdg_sql)
#Convert the merged dynlib into spectra object
dy_sps <- sql_to_spectra(ftflax_maize_hdg_sql)
available_spectrum_types(con_all)
accession_to_compid(ftflax_maize_hdg_sql, compound_accession = '101280')
```

the new compound_id that correspond to 101280 in the merged database is 88410.
Extrat the ms_compound table of that compound
```{r}
get_compound(ftflax_maize_hdg_sql, 88410)
```

Extrat the corresponding msms_spectrum table 
```{r}
get_spectrum_id(ftflax_maize_hdg_sql, 88410)
```

Use `MultMatchCID_Spectra()` to perform the CID spectral matching of 101280  
compound from ftms negative database:
```{r}
cmp <- MultMatchCID_Spectra(
  dy_sps,
  88410,
   spectrum_type_query = "individual",
  spectrum_type_target = "individual",
   ms_level_query = 3,
   ms_level_target = c(2,3,4),
  polarity_query = 0,
  polarity_target = 0,
  tolerance = 0.04,
  ppm = 10,
  minIons = ,
  fragments_resolution = "unit.resolution",
  requirePrecursor = T,
)
#sort the results based on the highet number of common ion
cmp_sorted <- cmp[order(cmp$ComIons, decreasing = TRUE, na.last = TRUE), ]
head(cmp_sorted, 5)
```
The highest match with 23 common ion corresponds to the **[herbacetin 3,8-di-o-beta-d-glucopyranoside ID AM]**: compound_id 88041.

Extract the corresponding ms_compound table of that compound:
```{r}
get_compound(ftflax_maize_hdg_sql, 88041)
```
'RD-20260907-1ODJ9T-101307' is the corresponding compound accession

# Plotting spectra and metabolome networks

we plot the spectra of that highest match:
```{r}
MSnplot_SQL(ftflax_maize_hdg_sql, 88041, thr_int = 100)
```
```{r}
plotMSn(ftflax_maize_hdg_sql,
                    compound_id = 88041,
                    prcx = 0.6,
                    thr_int = 0,
                    label_peaks = TRUE,
                    thr_label = 5,
                    digits = 0,
                    max_cols = 2,
                    spectrum_id = NULL)
```


Spectra of 88410:
```{r}
MSnplot_SQL(ftflax_maize_hdg_sql, 88410, thr_int = 100)
```

The spectral comparison reveals a high degree of similarity between the query compound and the reference compound 88041, annotated as herbacetin '3,8-di-O-β-D-glucopyranoside'. The MS3 spectra exhibit nearly identical precursor m/z values (463.04 and 463.08), with 23 common fragment ions and a dot product similarity score of 1.00, indicating a strong agreement between their fragmentation patterns.

Visual inspection of the spectra further supports this result, particularly through the presence of dominant fragment ions around m/z 300–301 and several additional shared fragments. Among the identified matches, compound 88041 shows the highest number of common fragment ions, providing stronger evidence of spectral similarity than the other candidate matches.

See **Spectra_networks_plots.qmd** workflow for more plotting possibilities and metabolome networks.

# Compound annotation in RDynLib

## Add provisional names from stored matches

`adding_Names_SQL()` adds a provisional name prefixed with `!` and records the supporting match as an annotation event. This example uses the working copy containing the stored FTneg MS² hits and preserves existing names.

```{r}
adding_Names_SQL(con_fqt,  spectrum_type = "same_energy", msLevel = 2, compound_id = NULL,
    overwrite = FALSE )
```

Adding names in ftms

```{r}
adding_Names_SQL(con_fft,  spectrum_type = "individual", msLevel = 2, compound_id = NULL,
    overwrite = FALSE )
```

## Transfer annotations between aligned databases
After testing the different types of the alignement functions in RDynlib, now we can transfer the names of the aligned compounds between databases: We test the function on the flax ftms data

```{r}
dir <- here("data")
SubDBNameTransfer_SQL(sqlite_dir = dir,  assoc_path = alignment_output )
```


## Curate a compound name interactively
Use EnterName_SQL() to update a compound name in DynLib and record structural information such as the following.
- Molecular formula
- Adduct type
- SMILES notation
This manual curation step lets you refine tentative annotations transferred in the previous sections.
```{r}
#| eval: false
EnterName_SQL(ft_path, CoMPID = 101280)
```

#Annotation history

Use `add_annotation_event()` to record curated evidence and its provenance from the example CSV. The CSV must use compound IDs from the database receiving the events.

```{r}
annotation_csv <- file.path(data_dir, "annotation_history_final.csv")
if (file.exists(annotation_csv)) {
    add_annotation_event(sql_path = annotation_db, csv_file = annotation_csv)
} else {
    message("Add annotation_history_final.csv to data/ to run the history import.")
}
```
